So one of the things about my job is I talk with a lot of auto insurance adjusters and lawyers (defense counsel and bus bench/billboard ambulance chasers). Here's some reality about car accidents and insurance they shared with me.

#1 Buy as much insurance as you can afford. Why? So if you kill somebody, you don't lose your house. Is this likely? Not really, juries & judges are reluctant to bankrupt normal people without much and if this happens, usually your insurance company will pick up the slack to avoid a bad faith lawsuit. 

BUT if you have state minimum limits or a low policy, you insurance company will want to get get rid of the claim as soon as possible. They're not going to fight for a dude with a $15k minimum if there's a chance they could have to pay an excess judgement for you. You'd be surprised at how little police/insurance have to do with each other because the claim won't be defended against so the reconstructionist/investigator isn't needed for anything other than the initial report. Often we'd meet the property damage adjuster so he could photograph a vehicle in evidence and that's the last we'd hear from an insurance company.

Also a fun fact: if you have a minimum property damage policy, State Farm will sue you for the difference after they take everything your policy has to offer...even though they themselves sell minimum policies.

#2 as an investigator with the sheriff's dept/office I've NEVER talked to an insurance agent. Your insurance agent doesn't actually care; they are there to play nice to sell you insurance. It's the adjusters on the phone who work your claim. Your agent is a whore for commission and has very little to do beyond filing a claim for you. 

#3 the police's collision report and the insurance investigation are two different things. Police look for criminal liability and insurance civil liability. Civil liability is nuanced and complex. I've only ever put an associated factor down on a TC report, never "47% at fault for violating CVC 222106(b), turning right on a Sunday."

#4 insurance adjusters usually know you're at fault when you call, especially if you get a ticket. But fun fact! In many states, like California, you don't automatically get a ticket if the cop feels you're at fault. (This was pre-woke policy in my dept's case)

#5 a total loss doesn't mean you get your money back, dollar for dollar. It's like "well you could have been totally screwed, but here, have some money so you aren't totally screwed." You don't get your down payment back, you get paid for the value of the vehicle just before the accident, you don't get replacement value, and every penny you put in for modifications or whatever doesn't necessarily result in being repaid for your cool rims or whatever. And you're not getting paid for regular maintenance. 

#6 the police don't actually care what happens with your insurance. They'll release the vehicle, the report, testify if required, but the police have a different job and only interact with insurance in MAJOR cases where serious felonies or death is involved. The police will not reinvestigate your dumb little accident because you "feel" you aren't at fault. 

#7 your insurance didn't screw you. You don't understand how the process works and you're just pissed off. Also, the police aren't out to get you or believe the other guy because reasons. You're just dumb and in the wrong.

#8 most people are stupid and don't know what happened in an accident. See my post on dashcams. Also people are FAR more honest on scene to police than they are after-the-fact to insurance. This is a long one. Fellow veterans, mutuals, I would greatly appreciate a retweet on this one. This is the only time you'll ever see me ask for one -- but be sure to read this first. It pertains to you, too. It's about my ongoing nightmare with the VA's Chapter 31 VR&E. 

For the rest of you, have you heard of the epidemic of America’s Armed Forces veterans driving up to a VA campus parking lot, and ending themselves in their own vehicles?

It’s so bad that even the Washington Post took a breather from its usual TDS to report about this tragic phenomenon during Trump’s first administration. http://Onceasoldier.com has its own section detailing these very specific occurrences as well. Why does this happen?

This much is certain: The veterans taking their own lives in this manner have grown so frustrated by inaction or denial by the VA that they lost all hope, they grew tired of the constant battle of dealing with the VA – and they wanted to send a message. And so they tragically ended themselves to send this very message.

If you had any idea just how stratified and inaccessible the VA is when it comes to communication, you’d be floored. Every VA campus has one single phone number acting as gatekeeper to any and all calls coming in. A few VAs actually circumvent this gatekeeping to better serve veterans. Most don’t.

The VA doesn’t want to listen, and they’ve become very good at figuring out ways to not listen.

Now when it comes to healthcare, the VA is solid. Especially when it comes to necessary healthcare and urgent care. Not every VA is as good as another, though and just about every vet who’s been to several will tell you this. But in this context I’ve found the VA to be consistent. If I was sick and showed up to every VA medical-capable installation I’ve been to, I was always taken care of immediately.

So why are these veterans ending themselves in this very specific manner, if their immediate healthcare is good? It’s mostly due to the benefits and occupational support side of the VA which are a different beast entirely. Applying for benefits with the VA is rarely ever a quick and painless procedure and more of a battle of attrition. Due to the changes that came along with the Trump Administration, claims have been processed far, far quicker than they ever have before and that’s fantastic. But a quickly processed claim does not mean it was a properly processed claim, and more often than not, the veteran has to get lawyers involved in order to for this proper processing to occur. This in itself is a problem, because most veterans can’t afford a lawyer, and most lawyers who work on a basis where they only bill the veteran upon a successful claim and resulting payout. The firms that specialize in this are very selective about which cases they take – and this isn’t the fault of the veteran. But that selective nature of these firms makes for basic business sense, as cold as that sounds.

Even this process is fraught with obstacles and denials by the VA, and many veterans who qualify for disability benefits fall through the cracks and end up frustrated, dejected, and driven to deliver a notice to the VA regarding their suffering in the aforementioned tragic fashion. Despite the recent drastic improvements to the VA’s claims handling, this still happens far too often.

Disability benefits aren’t the only aspect of the VA suffering from an awful process that drives veterans to despair or worse. There’s the other benefits and services that the VA offers to its vets. One of them is VR&E, and I’m going to describe the nightmare I’m still dealing with that particular section of the VA. 
 
VR&E -- aka Chapter 31 -- stands for Veteran Readiness and Education. It’s a department that offers what sounds like a fantastic resource for (further) education at accredited institutions provided the veteran in question qualifies for this service with the addition of a monthly living stipend during education/training. If you’re interested in what the requirements are, go look them up yourself, because this post is going to be long as it is. Needless to say, I qualified. I would be a fool to turn down such an opportunity, so I applied.  
 
When you qualify for VR&E, you are assigned a counselor from the VR&E department, and the counselor then tells you what is required to get the process rolling.  I applied for VR&E this same time last year with the intent of attending Texas Tech for the Spring 2026 semester (For those of you about to suggest the Hazlewood Act, I did not enlist in Texas.) My first counselor was Janice Adams of Detroit, Michigan -- as I was resident of Michigan at the time -- and my intent was to finish out my Mathematics degree. Janice informed me that this intent is acceptable under the VR&E program, and my first order of business was to apply to Texas Tech as a returning undergrad. Which I did, immediately – as soon as I wrapped up my call with Janice. 
 
The thing about applying with Chapter 31 benefits at any university is the application fee is waived. Or maybe that’s just Texas Tech. Regardless, fee-waiving is a process in itself that takes time. In this case, from the moment I finished talking to Janice, and the hour or so later that I finished the application and submitted it to Tech. 
 
This is where the problems started. I had no idea that this was going to be the tip of a very large, jagged iceberg. 
 
After what took about two weeks, I received an email from Texas Tech informing me that my application was accepted and the fee was waived. In less than 20 minutes – I am not exaggerating or lying here -- after I received my registration confirmation from Texas Tech, Janice emailed me informing me, with zero prior warning, that she dropped me from VR&E. The reason? I hadn’t “fulfilled requirements” with an approved application. 
 
In every conversation and communication I’ve had with Janice from the moment I qualified for Chapter 31 to that moment, never once did she inform me that there was a deadline for this application – not that there was one.  My sole notification of yet another one of these deadlines was her unilateral decision to drop me from the program and that was that. I tried calling her back, no answer. It was a Friday afternoon, and she probably already took the afternoon off. In a panic, I contacted Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin’s office that very day and explained my issue. 
 
Senator Slotkin’s office responded immediately and broke through the stratified layers that enshroud the VA that following Monday. I don’t know what her office said to the VA, but Janice called me back and in the most apologetic manner imaginable, going so far as to say that she’s been my “best friend” during this whole process -- which is odd considering how limited our communication has been up to that point – but whatever. She informed me that my case was reopened and I was reinstated to Chapter 31. 
 
Thank you for your rapid response on that, @SenatorSlotkin. I truly mean that. You have been the only one who actually did anything to help me during this entire ordeal and you office was lightning quick in response as well. 

I’d like to stop and point out two things: first, I had to involve a politician from DC in order to fix Janice Adam’s callous attempt to dismiss me. A state senator. This bears repeating: I had to contact a state senator who was currently working in DC in order to make the VA do their job correctly – and that’s not the even the craziest thing. I had to contact another politician in DC later regarding the same inexcusable conduct of this very same VR&E representative, Janice Adams. Why? This is insane. 
 
Second, Senator Slotkin’s intervention had my case reopened, after it was closed. The reason I mention this second detail will be relevant later.

I then followed every directive and requirement that Janice required of me before January 2026 came about; and before I even applied for Chapter 31, I did my research on everything this department would possibly need to in order to process my enrollment. I went so far as to even provide Janice with my intended route to return to Texas and even included the hotels I intended to overnight at. I was as thorough as possible. I did not slack on anything, especially when it came to whatever Janice requested from me. And I saved every single communication I had with Janice because I’ve dealt with the VA before, and I knew better than to not keep receipts of everything. My VR&E folder where I keep all my communications since start of this nightmare this time last year is currently 45MB.

There was one requirement that I couldn’t provide to Janice until I actually reached Texas Tech, however. And I made this very clear to Janice before I left, before Janice wishing me a safe and happy trip.

The reason I couldn’t provide that information is because I’m a returning undergrad, and returning undergrads are prioritized the same as freshmen when it comes to registration access. What this means is seniors get the first pick of the classes, followed by juniors, followed by the freshmen – and the freshmen are only given the three days before the start of the semester to register. This is policy at Texas Tech. Like I said: I informed Janice of this.

And, I’m a senior. That means not every course I might require to graduate will be available for one of two reasons: It’s either already filled up by seniors who were able to register a month before I was and the second being or it’s a course limited to either the Fall or Spring semesters. So, after I loaded up my home into the U-Haul, I high-tailed it to Lubbock and made it here on January 8th. On that next day, Friday January 9th, I went and visited my Mathematics Undergrad Advisor who was there during my previous attendance and is one of the most incredibly wonderful people I’ve ever encountered in academia. Within minutes, she showed me what my options were, and what classes I needed in order to graduate within the next two semesters. She registered me, and I was off to the races.

Or so I thought.

That evening when I returned to my hotel room (I still had to find a place to live), I checked my email.

Janice Adams had sent me an email while I was visiting with Patty. In said email, Janice announced that she dropped me from VR&E. Again. The reason being: I hadn’t turned in my degree plan yet. Gotta love how Catch-22 is still government policy over at the VA. Also within hours of receiving said requirement. Unbelievable.  I can’t think of a truer metaphor for this than Charlie Brown trying to kick the football held by Lucy than my own dealings with Janice Adams. She somehow managed to pull the football away at the very last second, both times.

This means that Texas Tech wasn’t being paid, and that I wasn’t going to get my stipend. All because Janice Adams couldn’t wait the few hours for me to report back with that information that I told her I would get to her later that day.

And no, she did not answer her phone that day. Nor did she respond to my emails. There was no valid reason Janice Adams can possibly make as to not allow me the few hours to forward that information to her. None whatsoever.

And now that I thnk about it, there’s no reason whatsoever that VR&E counselors should be able to unilaterally decide to cut off a veteran with not even a SINGLE warning. If there’s one thing that needs to be changed to Chapter 31, it’s this. There should be at least three warnings via e-mail, verbally by phone, or by snail mail that a veteran is liable to be removed from VR&E for lack of certain documentation.

On Monday morning, I visited the Lubbock VA and immediately coordinated with the VR&E case worker there. She told me that this sort of thing has happened before, and that I’d have to fill out ANOTHER application for VR&E, and that they could retroactively backdate the tuition and stipend payouts, and that I should be okay. It might take up to 120 days, she informed me.

That’s four months without Texas Tech receiving their tuition and me not receiving my monthly stipend – but Texas Tech understood my issue and let me attend anyway. I had credit cards that I kept and used only for emergencies. So with what little money I had left, I found a small home to rent and started to live as sparingly as I could off my credit cards.

I also didn’t sit on my laurels. I contacted anyone and everyone I could find related to VR&E in Texas and begged them to speed up my application and get me with a counselor and in the middle of March, my application was accepted yet again and I had to yet again attend the same VR&E online orientation courses that I took months prior.

My new counselor was Andrietta Gayles, and in my first discussion with Andrietta, I told here what the situation was and that I really, really need to get that tuition paid and my stipends paid out. Andrietta asked me to send her the tuition bill, which I did. And then Andrietta coldly informed me that they can’t cover prior tuition bills – and that all she can do is handle my application for the upcoming Fall semester. This contradicts what my Lubbock VR&E rep informed me earlier.

For any of you who have attended university in this country, you will know that Tech’s generosity to me in regards to this tuition bill is not common. If you don’t pay within so many days of the beginning of the semester, they drop you and remove all access to Webwork and your email and your ability to simply attend class. And you also know that if you have an outstanding bill with them, YOU CANNOT REGISTER FOR THE NEXT SEMESTER.

So, I return to my VR&E rep at the Lubbock VA several times. Nothing is done. 
 
I recently finished my semester with passing grades on everything, but my tuition still hasn’t been paid. My stipends haven’t been paid out yet. My credit cards are maxed. 
 
Around finals week, I get a notice from Andrietta that she dropped me from VR&E because I didn’t fulfill certain requirements about my degree plan and registration. Which is a moot point because I can’t attend next semester without that tuition paid.

Did I mention Andrietta claims to have a PhD? That means she is aware of this. She knows the process. But she didn’t care.

I then did what I had to do while back in Michigan – I contacted the office of a DC politician, Representative Jodey Arrington. I detailed what the problem was and turned over my 45MB archive of ALL my communication up to this point with VR&E.

A week or so ago his office responded to me that the VA gave him the same run-around that Andrietta gave me and told me I need to fill out another VR&E application and start the 120-day process all over again. 

The other day, I visit the VR&E rep again, futile as that was. I told her I need to talk to someone above her. A supervisor. It’s been over six months, this issue can be easily and quickly resolved by re-opening my previously closed case and approving it. She gave me the phone number to one of her superiors in El Paso.

Once I contact this supervisor, I spent about half of an hour detailing everything you’ve read up to this point.
And guess what he told me to do? Go on. Take a wild guess.

He told me to fill out an application and there is a 120 day wait – which entails me having to also go through the entire orientation again.  He also told me he can’t re-open my case, which we know isn’t true because my case has been re-opened before. He just doesn’t want to.
 
Finally, the other day, I went in and talked to the same lady running VR&E at the Lubbock VA – the same one whom I went to this past January after Janice Adams wrongfully dropped, agreed I was wrongfully dropped, and told me that this sort of thing will be fixed in due order – and guess what she told me.

“There’s a process. You need to fill out another application, and it may take up to 120 days.”
 
What is my recourse here? Nothing. I’ve put in for a higher-level review (with myself present) but that was months ago and I haven’t received anything back from the VA by phone, mail, or email. As I’ve stated many times before, the VA is so stratified that talking to someone who isn’t trained to respond like a robot is next to impossible. And I don’t have 120 days anymore. The Fall semester starts in less than two months. The two local VR&E reps here know this, and they don’t care. 
 
It’s been six months. Six months. That’s how long I’ve been holding out, waiting for the VA to realize that this is a mistake on their end and not due to inaction on mine.

So is my issue here as bad as a combat vet suffering from a blown out back or knees or a nagging combat injury that worsens over time? No. It’s certainly not. But my issue here is typical of the red tape run-around that many VA employees still force veterans to suffer to get anything accomplished. Many VA employees and reps care. I just happened to find a holdout of the ones who don’t. 
 
And Janice axed me from VR&E with zero warning not once, but twice. You read that correctly: Zero warning. And both of these times weren’t because of anything I forgot or failed to do, yet she dishonestly claimed as much and eliminated my enrollment regardless. Now imagine if there are veterans out there with, for example, PTSD issues that affect their memory; and they’re trying to make use of Chapter 31 only to forgot a single document that Janice dishonestly claimed I had. They would get axed from the program too, with zero warning. Zero recourse. This is unacceptable.

The entire point is thus: If this is happening to me, it’s happening to other veterans whose health and situations are far more dire than mine. 
 
I qualified for Chapter 31. I was approved for Chapter 31. I fulfilled every requirement of Chapter 31. And due to their inaction or malfeasance or stupidity, they still screwed me over. I now have a $9,000 unpaid tuition bill from Tech and destroyed credit. 

A $9,000 tuition bill and destroyed credit. That's what I have to show for trusting the VA. 
 
So am I going to game-end myself in the VA parking lot? No. But I now I have a better understanding why these other veterans lose all hope and that drastic, final, tragic message is their last resort and after reading this, and I hope you do too. I can’t even begin to imagine a veteran struggling with severe PTSD issues or chronic pain and having to deal with the same do-nothing mindsets that I’ve dealt with for the past six months.

The VA’s VR&E program needs the same sort of shakedown and culling that the rest of the VA recently experienced. It needs qualified and capable representatives in that section that can identify and handle issues like mine – because if there’s one thing I learned, if the VA screwed me over in this regard, they probably screwed hundreds of other veterans over in this regard as well --  and who have simply given up and don’t know what else to do. And that’s the other point of this long-winded post, aside from getting more eyes on this problem.

-Ethan Forsythe
6/18/2026

🧵 India's biggest-ever SME IPO opens this week. 
Q-Line Biotech (#QLine): set to raise ₹214 Cr. of fresh issue with marquee anchor investors (#abakkus #carnelian #HDFC #360One) & many more. 
Skip the hype and a deep dive into RHP raises serious concerns investors need to consider while evaluating the IPO for investment

🚩A company that sells 65% to its own group → guarantees ₹46 Cr of that  group's debt → can't convert profit to cash → sits on 10 months of  inventory → gets downgraded 4 notches by CRISIL → shares an office with an  IT-raided entity it claims to have exited → belongs to a group named in a  ₹500–700 Cr pathology scam → and books a ₹17 Cr loss it won't explain.

🚩 #1 — It sells 65% to its own group: POCT Services
283 distributors on paper. In reality, one group entity — POCT Services —  absorbs more than 60%+ of all sales.  
% revenue share, year by year: 
▪ FY23: 37.9% 
▪ FY24: 51.7% 
▪ FY25: 62.9% 
▪ 9M FY26: 65.4%  
This isn't a distribution network. It's a related party. And the  dependence deepens every single year — the opposite of what you want to  see before an IPO.

🚩 #2 — It also backstops that group's debt
It sells to the group. Does it also stand behind the group financially?  Yes.  
Corporate guarantees in the contingent-liability note: 
▪ POCT Science House: ₹10.6 Cr (Mar'25) → ₹15 Cr (Dec-25) 
▪ POCT Services: ₹31.05 Cr (brand new in Dec-25) 
▪ Total: ₹46 Cr — up from ZERO in FY23 & FY24  
See the loop: Q-Line books revenue selling to POCT, and simultaneously  guarantees POCT's borrowings. Revenue and risk circulate inside the same  family. If POCT stumbles, Q-Line — and now its public shareholders —  are on the hook

🚩 #3 — The profits don't become cash
A healthy business converts profit into cash. This one doesn't.  
Net cash from operations: 
▪ FY23: +₹25 Cr 
▪ FY24: −₹24 Cr ❌ 
▪ FY25: −₹1.3 Cr ❌ 
▪ 9M FY26: −₹33 Cr ❌  
Three straight years of negative operating cash flow — Reported profit on the P&L, real  cash walking out the door. 

🚩 #4 — Where the cash is trapped
It's stuck in receivables and inventory that keep swelling.  

Debtor days: 66 (FY23) → 96 (FY25) → 160 (Dec-25)
Inventory days: 180 (FY23) → 226 (FY25) → 305 (Dec-25)  
That's ~10 months of inventory sitting idle, and customers taking 5+ months to pay. 
Recall who the biggest customer is. 
And the company's own projections keep debtor days at 115 through FY28.  They aren't promising a fix — they're normalising the bloat.

🚩 #5 — CRISIL has already downgraded the credit rating
On April 9, 2026, CRISIL:  
▪ Cut long-term: BBB+/Stable → B/Stable (four notches) 
▪ Cut short-term: A2 → A4 
▪ Tagged it "Issuer Not Cooperating" — the company stopped sharing  information.
A four-notch downgrade, weeks before the IPO, and the firm went dark on  its own rating agency. Yet it's comfortable asking the public for ₹214  Cr.

🚩 #6 — The "clean exit" that wasn't
Now the governance gets uncomfortable.  
The Income Tax Dept ran search & seizure operations on POCT Science  House Pvt Ltd (Sep 2–5, 2025); books and records were impounded. 
Q-Line  says it divested its 49% stake on Mar 20, 2025 — a clean break.  
Except: 
▪ POCT Science House still operated from the SAME office as Q-Line 
▪ Its guarantee from Q-Line ROSE from ₹10.6 Cr (Mar'25) to ₹15 Cr (Dec'25) — AFTER the  supposed exit 
 If you've genuinely walked away, why the shared address — and why put  MORE money on the line for them?

🚩 #7 — And the group has a documented history
This is where it stops being about accounting.  An NDTV investigation (Sep 6, 2025) into Madhya Pradesh's govt pathology-lab scandal names the winning consortium as "Science  House Medicos and POCT Services." NDTV reported:  
▪ 85 govt labs billed at premium NABL rates — NONE were NABL-accredited  at contract start 
▪ Scam estimated at ₹500–700 Cr, with ≥₹300 Cr in overbilling 
▪ FDA-approved machines required, never used; single-bidder re-tender  rule ignored 
▪ Science House's promoter had served jail time for corruption; POCT  blacklisted in multiple states 
▪ The Economic Offences Wing had already filed a case  
"Science House" is a JV of Q-Line with its erstwhile associate POCT Science House.

Why is this budget so damaging ? (1/2)

When people hear that someone is running a business, they often assume that they are rich. It’s easy to see why: businesses have employees, shops, business premises, and vehicles, which all create an impressive image. However, the reality is often quite different. Let’s consider a scenario.

Imagine you operate a small engineering firm with nine engineers and one office staff member, generating an annual turnover of around one million pounds.

At first glance, a million pounds sounds a lot.

However, after accounting for expenses like materials, wages, rent, rates, insurance, utilities, vehicle upkeep, waste disposal, advertising, tools, IT services, phones, industry memberships, health and safety training, personal protective equipment, and accounting fees—the list goes on, trust me it does—the business is left with a profit margin of just 10%.

That translates to a profit of £100,000. Impressive, right? But let’s break it down further. First, there’s corporation tax, which amounts to £22,750. The owner might want to retain £25,000 in the business for unexpected expenses, and there are certainly many potential challenges—like having to pay employees to clean the yard, wash vehicles when there is no work or cover for overtime when there is too much. Not to mention the risk of not getting paid when a client goes bankrupt or misquoting a job (it happens). The list of uncertainties is long.

So, after accounting for the corporation tax and the rainy day fund, we’re left with £52,250. However, the owner still needs to pay themselves a wage this is usually by paying themselves a dividend; let’s say they aim for £50,000 (most do 60hr weeks) and this year they can. Dividend allowance now capped at £500, they’re left with no tax benefits for all the sleepless nights spent worrying about the business and paying everyone’s wages week in week for the last year. They’re just subject to more taxes, like everyone else.

Now, let’s assess the impact of this budget. Each employee at the company effectively faces an additional job tax of around £900, in addition to what the company already pays. For a company with ten employees, that totals £9,000. Importantly, this tax doesn’t come off the million-pound turnover; it’s deducted from the £100,000 net profit. This means the profit shrinks to £91,000. Now, the corporation tax drops to £20,365. Subtracting the rainy day fund and the owner’s salary leaves just £45,635. The owner is left with two choices: take a smaller dividend than the previous year or reduce the rainy day fund (which could be risky if a lathe breaks down or a delivery vehicle fails its MOT). Alternatively, they may have to raise prices, which ultimately impacts consumers—the ‘working people’ yes, like you and me.

This scenario can be applied across various businesses. While the numbers might differ, the situation remains same. Tax is tax no matter what the business. There are approximately 5.6 million small to medium enterprises (SMEs) in the UK, which serve as the backbone of the economy. Whether it’s your local butcher, baker, hairdresser, landlord or builder, these businesses face similar challenges. Some owners dream of achieving such profits as described above, while others might scoff at making so little, but either way, the additional tax burden on jobs reduces their bottom line and leaves many questioning, ‘what’s the point’. 

When a country’s entrepreneurs start thinking ‘What’s the point’ a country is in a very poor place.

I have spent over 7 years attacking healthcare revenue cycle and trying to simplify medical billing at @rivethealth. Billions before us, and surely after, have been invested to improve it. It's still really, really bad. An RCM outsider asked me in a very sincere manner earlier this week: “How is revenue cycle so bad and so hard when so many companies work on it?” Something about the way he asked the question has kept me thinking about this since. 

What do you think? 

Here's what AI had to say. I gotta say: it's not bad...

"Oh, this is such a good question. It’s honestly one of the most fascinating puzzles in healthcare. You’re right—saying “healthcare is hard” is a cop-out. It is hard, but so are a lot of things that have gotten dramatically better, faster, easier, and cheaper in the past decade.

So why doesn’t revenue cycle follow that arc?

Here’s a brain-dump of reasons, some obvious, some deeper, and some more “conspiracy-theory” flavored, in no particular order:

1. Misaligned Incentives
The players in the rev cycle “game” (providers, payers, vendors, patients) do not actually want the same outcomes. Most software eats industries by simplifying the connection between what people want and how to get it. In healthcare RCM, “optimizing” for one stakeholder often means adding friction for another.

Example: Payers want denials and slow payment to keep costs down; providers want fast, full payment; patients want clarity, but are a distant afterthought.
Vendors sometimes make money because the process is broken—not in spite of it.

2. Insane Fragmentation (a.k.a. “Everyone’s Special”)
Unlike, say, the credit card industry or e-commerce (which eventually converged on standards), healthcare rev cycle is an endless fractal of edge cases, local rules, payer quirks, regulatory overlays, contract idiosyncrasies, and weird IT stacks.

Even if you solve 99% of it, the last 1% is different for every hospital, every payer, every geography, every specialty.
“The same, but never the same.”
Fragmentation = endless opportunity for “point solutions” and no one can ever claim they’ve solved it all.

3. Legacy Everything
Every big provider, payer, and system is running on spaghetti code, mainframes, faxes, homegrown “add-ons,” and patchwork integrations.

New tech can’t just “replace” this. Everything has to interoperate or layer on top, which breeds complexity and, inevitably, bugs and inefficiency.
Technical debt in rev cycle is so deep that “rip and replace” is nearly impossible.

4. “Solving” Revenue Cycle is Not Always Good Business
Let’s be real: If anyone truly fixed revenue cycle, a lot of very profitable businesses would be out of business.

Many vendors are, at some level, financially incentivized for continued dysfunction—whether that’s explicit or just the reality of “change management as a service.”
Revenue cycle “complexity” is the moat for a lot of companies.

5. Inertia & Change Aversion
Large health systems, payers, and even small clinics are deeply risk-averse (sometimes for good reason: the risk is literally not getting paid at all).
Switching costs are huge—change management, retraining, and perceived risk often outweigh potential benefits.

6. “Solving” Revenue Cycle Isn’t a Purely Technical Problem
Even the most elegant, automated solution still has to be implemented by humans in hospitals, clinics, and call centers who may be underpaid, overworked, and stuck using whatever ancient EHR the C-suite bought in 2011.
Political battles over who “owns” the problem inside orgs often torpedo innovation.
No amount of AI can fix a denials team that’s on strike or a billing office that doesn’t want to change.

7. Perverse Feedback Loops
Success in revenue cycle is invisible (“hey, we got paid on time!” = crickets), but failure is very visible (“hey, where’s my $2M claim?” = all hands on deck).
This means investment often chases failure, not building for the long term.

8. Constantly Moving Target
Every year: new codes, new payer rules, new government requirements, new value-based whatever.
Vendors are always catching up, never caught up.

9. Lack of a True Platform/Network Effect
Most RCM vendors don’t own the transaction end-to-end and can’t create a true “network effect” (like Visa/Mastercard or Plaid in fintech).
The system is still “too balkanized” for a single player to reach critical mass.

10. “Nobody Actually Wants It to Be Easy” (Dark Horse Theory)
If claims were as simple as swiping a credit card, every tiny provider could survive, costs would drop, and massive incumbents would lose pricing power.
In some deep, unspoken way, the system is optimized for complexity, not simplicity.

11. The “Measurement Problem”
You can’t fix what you can’t measure, and “what is a clean claim rate?” or “what does it mean to get paid the right amount, on time?” is not well-defined across the ecosystem.
Everyone reports their own KPIs, and the numbers are often “managed” rather than transparent."

Post Office scandal: why is it taking so long to pay victims compensation? 

Only a quarter of the money set aside for victims of the @PostOffice scandal has been paid out, according to the latest data.

Complex schemes, legal wrangling and bureaucracy have been blamed for slow progress that has left more than 3,000 potential victims still waiting for a payout.
Postmasters started ringing alarm bell about the Horizon system in the early 2000s, but it was not until 2019 that a High Court case brought the scandal to public attention. Mr Justice Fraser ruled that Horizon was riddled with faults that could cause money to appear to have gone missing from Post Office branch accounts.

By then, nearly a thousand people had been convicted based on Horizon data and as many as 4,700 more had repaid money that appeared to be missing, or had been forced out of their businesses. Some had been made bankrupt.

Five years after the ruling, how many of these victims have received compensation? And why is it taking so long to pay redress to postmasters?

Horizon compensation by numbers

As of October 31, 2,765 out of about 5,700 possible victims had received full compensation, totalling £438 million. This was only a fraction of the £1.8 billion that has been put aside by @RachelReevesMP , the chancellor at @hmtreasury 

Many of those still fighting for their compensation are those worst affected by the scandal and with the largest claims, but others are those who simply submitted their applications late.

The various schemes paid out final compensation to 192 people in October. At this rate, it will take another 16 months to pay the remaining victims, although high-value disputes have tended to get snarled up for far longer.

Why has compensation been so slow?

Compensation had a slow start because of government tight-fistedness. The Bates group were told that their £11,500 per person settlement in 2019 was “full and final”, until @BorisJohnson caved under pressure a full three three years later.

The court process has also been slow. It took two years for the first case to go through, clearing 39, and even today only 111 convictions have been quashed in court. It was the realisation that this would never clear all the postmasters that led the Conservative government to pass the Post Office Offences Act on May 24. Reeves increased the compensation pot from £1 billion at the budget to account for the new beneficiaries resulting from the legislation.

The HSS, which has made better progress, was introduced in 2020 but many victims were not aware of its existence until the @ITV drama Mr Bates vs The Post Office made the scandal front page news. This helps to explain why more than 1,800 claims are still being worked on.

Aside from individual delays, the four schemes have all been criticised for being too complex. Each runs differently, with different legal parameters and appeals processes. However, they all involve long claim forms and demands for documents evidencing losses running back decades. They have been set up to be adversarial and bureaucratic, meaning that lawyers on both sides rack up huge fees arguing over minutiae.

@KemiBadenoch , the former business secretary and now leader of the Conservative Party, blamed the “government machine” for slow progress when she gave evidence to the Post Office inquiry this week, saying that her predecessors had allowed “bureaucracy to get in the way” of compensation. In short, that the schemes were flawed by design.

She said contemporaneous emails showed that she “wanted to get the money out there” but had been “always given a reason why we couldn’t” by government officials.

She spoke about how red tape was slowing up payments. “I think I remember asking a question like, ‘Why can’t we just give them the money?’,” she said.

 “Then I’d be told there could be a judicial review and the Treasury has these value for money requirements — if you don’t meet them then you might end up having to go to court — so I just kept trying to find a way through.”

PART IV: THE MSO STRUCTURE - SEPARATING ECONOMICS FROM LIABILITY

This is what separates good operators from great operators in healthcare.

Corporate practice of medicine laws prevent non-licensed individuals from owning medical practices in most states.
The stated purpose: prevent business interests from interfering with clinical decisions.
The actual effect: creating entity structuring opportunities for sophisticated operators.

The constraint: You can't directly own the entity that employs clinicians and bills for services.

The solution: Management Services Organization (MSO) structure.
You create two legal entities:

Clinical Practice PC (owned by licensed providers):

Employs all clinical staff

Holds medical licenses

Bills for patient services
Provides all patient care
Has all regulatory compliance obligations

Carries all clinical liability

One or two of your lead clinicians own this entity (you help them set it up, they own it legally).

Management Services Organization LLC (owned by you):

Owns all hard assets (medical equipment, IT systems, furniture, possibly real estate)

Provides all administrative services (facilities, billing, collections, marketing, HR, IT, compliance support)

Employs all administrative staff

Has no patient contact

Provides no clinical services

You own this entity 100%.

The two entities are connected by a Management Services Agreement (MSA).

The MSA specifies:

MSO provides all administrative services

Clinical Practice pays MSO a management fee

Management fee is typically 88-92% of collections after direct clinical labor costs

The Financial Structure:
Let's walk through how money flows:
Medicaid pays $118 to Clinical Practice for a patient visit.
Clinical Practice pays:
Clinician compensation: $40 (proportional cost for that visit)
MSO management fee: $72 (92% of the $78 remaining after clinical comp)
Clinical Practice retains: $6

The Clinical Practice keeps $6 per visit to cover their minimal overhead (professional liability insurance, some administrative costs, licensing fees).

The MSO receives $72 per visit.
Out of that $72, the MSO pays:
Facilities/rent: $8
Medical supplies/equipment: $3
Administrative staff: $15
Billing/collections: $6

Marketing: $3

IT systems: $4

Compliance/consulting: $3
Total MSO costs: $42
MSO EBITDA: $30 per visit
At 4,100 visits annually (your current volume):

Clinical Practice EBITDA: $24,600 annually (split among the 2 provider-owners) MSO EBITDA: $1.23M annually (to you)

Total business EBITDA: $1.25M

Wait, that's less than the $1.59M we calculated before. Let me recalculate.

The issue is I'm mixing per-visit economics with business-level economics. Let me approach it differently:
Business-Level Financial Structure:
Annual revenue: $4.62M
Under previous structure (you own everything):

Total costs: $3.03M (clinical salaries, facilities, admin, everything)

EBITDA: $1.59M (to you)

Under MSO structure:
Clinical Practice:
Revenue: $4.62M (from Medicaid)
Clinical salaries paid: $1.64M
MSO management fee paid: $2.73M (92% of the $2.98M remaining after clinical salaries)
Retained by Clinical Practice: $250K (covers their insurance, licensing, minimal overhead, and small profit for provider-owners)
MSO (owned by you):
Revenue: $2.73M (management fees from Clinical Practice)
Costs: $1.42M (facilities, admin staff, supplies, marketing, IT, compliance - everything except clinical salaries)

EBITDA: $1.31M

Total EBITDA of combined entities: $1.31M (MSO) + $250K (Clinical Practice) = $1.56M

(Slightly less than the $1.59M in the previous structure due to some inefficiency in having two entities, but close enough)
Here's what this structure accomplished:

You (MSO owner) capture: $1.31M (84% of total EBITDA) Providers (Clinical Practice owners) capture: $250K (16% of total EBITDA)

The providers think they "own the practice" because their names are on the Clinical Practice entity.

They're making good money ($125K each if split between two providers, on top of their clinical salaries).

But you own:

All the hard assets

All the systems and infrastructure
The entity that extracts 84% of the profit
More importantly:

All clinical and regulatory liability stays with the Clinical Practice:

Malpractice claims → Clinical Practice and individual providers
Regulatory investigations → Clinical Practice
Licensing issues → Clinical Practice
Medicare/Medicaid compliance audits → primarily Clinical Practice
Your MSO just provides administrative services:

No clinical decision-making
No patient care
Just business operations
If something goes catastrophically wrong, your MSO can terminate the Management Services Agreement and walk away with your assets and infrastructure intact.

You've separated economics (which you control) from liability (which providers bear).

House MD is a great show about the adventures of a monster truck-loving Sherlock expy and his homoerotic relationship with his oncologist bestie, BUT IT’S ALSO A DOODOO REPRESENTATION OF HOSPITAL MEDICINE, SO HERE’S HOW MY JOB IS DIFFERENT FROM A TV SHOW🗒️

I’m a hospitalist: the primary doctor assigned to a hospitalized patient. I’m the shotcaller of the medical team responsible for diagnosing & treating their acute care conditions, coordinating procedures or surgeries with the specialists I bring onboard, and piloting the patient’s hospital stay from admission to discharge. A lot of people are unfamiliar with how hospital (inpatient) medicine is different from clinic (outpatient) medicine, so I usually explain it like “I’m kind of like House.” With a few differences:

1) WHERE ARE YOUR PATIENTS MAN
It’s probably narratively much easier to follow, but House only gets to be responsible for ONE patient each episode (which usually lasts a few days). In real life, your average hospitalist is carrying somewhere from 16-22 patients at a time, with new admissions coming in and discharges going out on the daily. It’s even a major plot point in Season One where Vogler is looking at things and he’s literally like wtf this whole thing is bleeding money. He also grills Cuddy for letting House have a made-up Department of Diagnostic Medicine just because he’s so smart and fancy like I get it man I think having an entire department dedicated to treating one patient a week is crazy too

2) NAME A SINGLE NON-DOCTOR ON THIS SHOW
Ok but like where the hell are the social workers throughout the entire hospital??? Probably the most important people I have to answer to as a doctor are the case managers who are assigned to each patient in the hospital. They’re the ones who navigate the patient’s insurance and setup the delivery of their oxygen tanks, wheelchairs, or home infusions. I literally cannot discharge patients from the hospital until the social worker actually gives me the green light, or else I get shit on and guilt tripped for almost causing a lawsuit for an unsafe discharge. Hospital medicine has SO many moving parts, and just cause doctors are off doing their own thing and saving lives and blah blah blah you literally don’t get anywhere unless your case manager is in the loop and literally taking care of the whole hospitalization outside the medicine.

3) WHO GAVE YOU PERMS
House’s team is under “diagnostic medicine,” but apparently they’re also credentialed to do all of their own surgeries, biopsies, imaging, breaking into patients’ houses, etc. In real practice, all of these jobs are specialized and done by different services. A surgery is done by a consulting surgeon, a CT is done by an imaging technician, a transthoracic echocardiogram is done by an ultrasound technician, a transesophageal one is done by a cardiologist. In general, every specialization has their role, and medicine’s is to figure out the patient’s “Why.” Modern hospital practices have practically eliminated the hospitalist’s responsibility to do procedures, as well. For example, at the hospital I did residency in, we had entire teams of nurse practitioners and physician assistants whose entire jobs were to place central lines, do thoracenteses, or get LP’s: back in the day, this was internal medicine bread and butter. There’s a pretty good Conan Liu video about this (resident education has suffered a LOT because of recent ABIM changes), but basically, everything has just become streamlined towards the diagnostics. As a hospitalist, my job is a lot more like a detective than the crime scene crew. I’m here to interpret results in the context of the diagnostic picture, rather than physically obtaining them; or figuring out what should be the correct treatment, rather than actually administering it. There are so many times in the show when the doctors are shown drawing their own labs or pushing their own meds instead of the nurses and I’m like “haha wtf I don’t even know how to start a drip on an Alaris pump.” (I’ve literally never started a bag on a pump before)

4) WHY DOES EVERYONE DO EVERYTHING
In the lore, House is dual-boarded in infectious disease and nephrology (both fellowships that come after completion of an internal medicine residency), but also did a pathology residency for some reason? But basically practices as a clinical internist, plus handles inpatient and outpatient duties every episode?? Obviously Wilson is an oncologist, the show does mention that Cuddy is an endocrinologist, Foreman is a neurologist, etc. But like without looking at the House wiki, can you even name what residencies/fellowship other characters like Chase, Cameron, or even Amber are? Chase has apparently done internal medicine residency, cardiology fellowship, AND a critical care fellowship, AND also did a year of neurosurgery in Australia?? Cameron is an immunologist???? Amber is interventional radiology????? I don’t think their specialties ever come up outside of a few suggested differentials (in the initial stages of an episode, and so usually wrong) and maybe a procedure or two. In real life, all of these specialties would be on separate teams, and individually consulted/brought on as the hospitalist deems it necessary. Or, if they were easy cases with a simple surgical fix, they would be admitted by those individual services and maybe a hospitalist would be consulted to manage their medical issues.

5) WHY ARE YOU EVEN TRAINEES ANYWAY
So like Princeton-Plainsboro Teaching Hospital is a TEACHING HOSPITAL right??? You’d think they would have residents and shit right? Like as far as the medical hierarchy goes, you have the medical student who is doing a rotation in the specialty (season 7 Dr. Masters); the resident, who has matched into the specialty and is learning how to practice independently (season 8 Dr. Park); the fellow, who has graduated residency and is certified for general practice of that specialty, but is continuing training in order to subspecialize in that field; and the attending (me) who leads the team and has the final say. Except in House, you realize that House is the attending, and all the people who work “underneath him” (IN COMPLETELY UNRELATED FIELDS) are his fellows??? Like they’re willingly sitting in there as trainees (working shit hours and not getting paid great money) just because House is some amazing doctor to train under??? It’s a big plot point in season 4 when Taub joins the team cause like bro if you were in private practice plastic surgery (literally making like $800k+) why the fuk would you go back to a teaching hospital to be a “diagnostic medicine” fellow. Even if your attending was some omniscient biblically-accurate angel who could teach you everything about life and the universe itself like what the helly half of these characters are literally fellowship-trained already

To the writers’ credit, depicting everything like the above would probably make for some really boring TV. As far as medical accuracy goes, House isn’t really terrible, but a lot of the eureka moments made right before the final diagnosis are sometimes super obvious buzzword-level associations that any preclinical medical student can figure out (e.g. the sporothrix episode lmao). If you want a better representation of inpatient medicine, Scrubs is still the most accurate show in my opinion. The Pitt is also a good one too, but also it’s about an emergency department, and I don’t touch downstairs medicine at all because those doctors are FREAKS
